decks.module: Residency, status and who needs licenses

cards.front: What makes someone a Florida resident for licensing?
cards.back: Florida residency means domiciling here over six straight months, registering to vote, or filing domicile or homestead papers.

cards.front: How do immigrants, non-immigrants and citizens differ?
cards.back: Immigrants are lawful permanent residents admitted by visa or USCIS adjustment, non-immigrants enter only briefly for a stated purpose, and citizens were born here or naturalized.

cards.front: Who must carry a Florida license, and who is excused?
cards.back: Residents must carry a Florida license on public roads, working or schooling newcomers within thirty days, while licensed visitors sixteen and up, federal crews, service families, and commuters are excused.

cards.front: Which other groups are exempt from holding a Florida license?
cards.back: College students, home-licensed migrant workers, and brief tractor or road-machine operators are also exempt.

cards.front: How does residency differ from the newcomer deadline?
cards.back: Residency turns on domicile, voting, or filings, while the thirty-day clock binds working or schooling newcomers only.
cards.memory_hook: Residency is status; clock binds workers

cards.front: What separates the three legal statuses?
cards.back: Immigrants hold permanent residence, non-immigrants visit briefly for a purpose, and citizens were born or naturalized here.

cards.front: When does a visitor's license alone let them drive here?
cards.back: A home-state license alone excuses a visitor sixteen or up, but an international permit works only beside the home-country license.

cards.front: Which outside licenses let a new resident skip Florida exams?
cards.back: Valid licenses from listed states, Canada, France, Taiwan, and Korea waive both Class E exams, German ones waive skills, vision still applies, and kept Canadian cards force testing.

cards.front: What does a Class E license cover?
cards.back: Class E covers non-commercial vehicles under twenty-six thousand one pounds; motorcycles over fifty cubic centimeters need an endorsement.
cards.memory_hook: Class E: under the commercial line

cards.front: What vehicles need a commercial license?
cards.back: Commercial licenses govern twenty-six thousand one-plus-pound rigs, sixteen-plus-passenger carriers, and placarded hazmat with vetting.

cards.front: How do the license-transfer waivers differ by origin?
cards.back: Most listed foreign and domestic licenses waive both Class E exams, German ones waive skills only, and kept Canadian cards force everything.

cards.front: Where does Class E end and commercial duty begin?
cards.back: Class E stops below twenty-six thousand one pounds while commercial duty starts there, at sixteen passengers, or with placarded cargo.

decks.module: Identity, Social Security and address proof

cards.front: What documents does every license applicant show?
cards.back: Applicants show primary identification, Social Security or secondary proof, and two address documents, all original, with a marriage, divorce, or court paper bridging name changes.

cards.front: How does a citizen prove primary identity?
cards.back: Citizens identify by government birth certificate, passport or card, consular report, or naturalization or citizenship certificate.

cards.front: How do immigrants and non-immigrants prove identity?
cards.back: Immigrants show green cards, passport stamps, or asylum or refugee grants; Canadians and non-immigrants show parallel papers.

cards.front: Which extra papers do students and exchange visitors add?
cards.back: Students add I-twenty forms, exchange visitors DS-two thousand nineteen forms, refugees extra papers, and travel, parole, and judge-order papers each ride with a passport.

cards.front: What may a non-citizen get while papers are checked?
cards.back: Non-citizens may draw a sixty-day photo-free temporary permit while agencies verify papers, denied if verification fails.

cards.front: How is a Social Security number proven?
cards.back: Social Security numbers are collected and verified; cards, W-two forms, full-number paychecks, one thousand ninety-nine forms, or military IDs prove them.

cards.front: Who must supply a secondary identification item?
cards.back: Numberless citizens and immigrants, plus all non-immigrants, supply one secondary item spanning licenses, military and school records, birth transcripts, seasoned life policies, draft and voter cards, court papers, foreign IDs, and weapon permits.
cards.memory_hook: No number means one more item

cards.front: Which papers can prove a residential address?
cards.back: Two address proofs come from leases, voter, vehicle, or vessel records, statements, utility hookups, booklets, service or medical cards, or insurance papers.

cards.front: What else can prove address, and what do housed applicants add?
cards.back: Transcripts, professional licenses, tax forms, exchange certificates, shelter letters, bank and government mail, and offender forms also prove address, and housed applicants add a host letter.
cards.memory_hook: Living with someone? Add host letter

cards.front: Which copies of documents are accepted or refused?
cards.back: Originals and certified copies pass, photocopies and notarized copies fail, and name gaps need a linking court or family paper.

cards.front: Can an applicant mix papers from different status tracks?
cards.back: Citizens, immigrants, Canadians, and non-immigrants each follow a separate primary-identification track with no mixing.

cards.front: What happens when verification of papers succeeds or fails?
cards.back: A sixty-day photo-free permit bridges agency verification, while failed primary and secondary checks end in denial.

cards.front: How many secondary items versus address papers are needed?
cards.back: Secondary identification needs one listed item for the numberless, while address proof always needs two residence papers.

cards.front: What does a learner need, and what does a first driver license need?
cards.back: Learners must be fifteen, trained, and vision- and knowledge-tested; drivers must be sixteen, identified, and skills-tested too.
cards.memory_hook: Learn at fifteen, drive at sixteen

cards.front: What must a minor complete before moving past the learner permit?
cards.back: Drivers under eighteen must hold a learner license for twelve months or until turning eighteen, whichever comes first, go twelve months without moving-violation convictions except one withheld adjudication, log at least fifty driving hours including ten at night certified by a parent, guardian, or responsible adult twenty-one or older, submit parental consent, and maintain school attendance.

cards.front: Who must take the substance-abuse course?
cards.back: The substance-abuse course binds every never-licensed applicant, except certified school driver-education graduates.

cards.front: What consent does an unmarried minor need?
cards.back: Unmarried minors need a signed parental application whose signer accepts responsibility and may rescind it to cancel; married and emancipated minors show certificates or court orders instead.

cards.front: What must drivers tell the state about their health?
cards.back: Drivers must disclose impairing conditions, secure a doctor report for seizures or blackouts, and may mark insulin dependence.

cards.front: What happens if you defy a license restriction?
cards.back: Defying a restriction draws a citation and suspension; letter codes cover lenses, hand controls, mirrors, daylight, and work limits.

cards.front: What do the numbered restriction codes order?
cards.back: Numbered codes order business-only routes, interlocks, alert bracelets, automatic gears, power steering, signals, grips, pedals, and hearing aids.

cards.front: How do learner entry and full licensure requirements differ?
cards.back: Learner entry opens at fifteen with training and two tests, and full licensure at sixteen adds identification plus the skills test.

cards.front: What does the teen licensure bundle include?
cards.back: Licensure under eighteen combines twelve months with a learner license or reaching age eighteen first, twelve conviction-free months aside from one withheld-adjudication moving violation, fifty practice hours with ten at night certified by a parent, guardian, or responsible adult twenty-one or older, parental consent, and school attendance compliance.

cards.front: Who skips the substance course?
cards.back: The substance course binds every never-licensed seeker, yet certified school driver-education graduates skip it.

cards.front: What does the consenting adult take on, and who bypasses consent?
cards.back: A consenting adult accepts driving responsibility and may rescind it to cancel, while married and emancipated minors bypass consent.

cards.front: How does an employment-only limit differ from business-only?
cards.back: Employment-only travel covers job trips while business-only reach extends to school, worship, and medical needs.

cards.front: What are the rules for Florida identification cards?
cards.back: ID cards start at age five, run four years for young holders and eight beyond, never coexist with a license, and go free to qualifying homeless and poverty-level applicants.

cards.front: How fast must career offenders register?
cards.back: Career offenders register in person within two working days and repeat at every renewal and address or name change.

cards.front: Who must meet draft or offender registration rules?
cards.back: Males eighteen to twenty-six must meet draft registration, and sexual offenders and predators must register within forty-eight hours.

cards.front: How are offender and predator cards marked?
cards.back: Offender cards print the statute tag and predator cards the predator label, and both groups report renewals and forty-eight-hour changes.

cards.front: What optional marks or gifts can be added at application?
cards.back: Donor registration, free veteran marks with discharge papers, and voluntary trust-fund gifts attach at application.

cards.front: How long do ID cards last, and can you hold one with a license?
cards.back: Identification cards run four years for the young and eight beyond, and no driver may hold a license and a card together.

cards.front: How do the career and sexual offender deadlines differ?
cards.back: Career offenders answer within two working days while sexual offenders and predators answer within forty-eight hours.

cards.front: What differs between offender and predator cards?
cards.back: Offender cards carry the statute tag while predator cards carry the predator label, and post boxes never count as home.

cards.front: What must you do after moving or changing your name?
cards.back: Address moves need a new license within thirty days via portal or office, and name changes ride on marriage, divorce, or court papers.

cards.front: What records must be fixed before a renamed card is issued?
cards.back: Social Security, immigration, and Canadian passport records must be corrected before Florida reissues a renamed card.

cards.front: How are lost cards replaced, and when is it free?
cards.back: Lost cards are replaced promptly in person or online, free for theft victims bearing a police report.

cards.front: Who must bring the full document set again?
cards.back: Full document sets return for anyone unissued since January one, two thousand ten, and non-immigrants renew and replace only in person.

cards.front: How long does a Class E license last, and who cannot renew?
cards.back: A Class E driver license remains valid for six to eight years; renewal requires presenting your old license and passing a vision exam, and is denied if you are ineligible, left a traffic summons unanswered, hold a suspended, revoked, or canceled license, or fail to present required documentation.

cards.front: Who may renew online, and what does lateness cost?
cards.back: Citizens and immigrants renew online for six or eight years unless remote-renewed before or disqualified, and late filings past the birthday deadline add fifteen dollars.

cards.front: What must drivers eighty and older do before renewing?
cards.back: Drivers eighty and older pass vision screening at no charge in person or by practitioner form before renewing.

cards.front: How soon after a move is a new license needed?
cards.back: Any address move forces a new license within thirty days, and a stale card risks missed mail plus a citation.

cards.front: What does renewal require, and who is barred?
cards.back: Class E renewal covers six to eight years upon showing your prior license and passing a vision exam, while ineligibility, an unanswered traffic summons, a suspended, revoked, or canceled license, or missing required documents prevents renewal.

cards.front: When is a replacement free, and when are full documents needed?
cards.back: Theft victims with a police report replace free, while the long-unissued must rebuild the full document set.

cards.front: Who is shut out of online renewal?
cards.back: Online renewal serves qualified citizens and immigrants but shuts out the recently remote-renewed and the suspended.

cards.front: What do licenses, permits, renewals, replacements and ID cards cost?
cards.back: First licenses, learner permits, and renewals cost forty-eight dollars; replacements and ID cards cost twenty-five dollars; late renewals add fifteen dollars.

cards.front: What are the reinstatement fees?
cards.back: Reinstatement costs one hundred eighty dollars for fraud, one hundred thirty dollars for substance offenses, seventy-five dollars after revocation, forty-five dollars after suspension, sixty dollars for most lapses, and fifty-five dollars for bad checks.

cards.front: What do insurance lapses cost to cure?
cards.back: Insurance lapses cost fifteen dollars for liability and one hundred fifty dollars, two hundred fifty dollars, then five hundred dollars across PIP suspensions inside three years, DUI cases included.

cards.front: What do retests, endorsements and collector service cost?
cards.back: Knowledge retests cost ten dollars, skills retests twenty dollars, endorsements seven dollars, and collector service six dollars and twenty-five cents; fully disabled veterans pay no license or ID fees.

cards.front: How do issue, replacement and late fees compare?
cards.back: Licenses and renewals cost forty-eight dollars, replacements and ID cards twenty-five dollars, and late renewals add fifteen dollars.

cards.front: How do revocation, suspension and fraud reinstatement fees compare?
cards.back: Revocation cures at seventy-five dollars, suspension at forty-five dollars, and most payment lapses at sixty dollars against fraud at one hundred eighty dollars.

cards.front: How do liability and injury-protection lapse fees compare?
cards.back: Liability lapses cure at fifteen dollars while injury-protection tiers climb one hundred fifty dollars, two hundred fifty dollars, then five hundred dollars inside three years.

cards.front: How do knowledge and skills retest fees compare?
cards.back: Knowledge retests cost ten dollars against twenty dollars for skills, and fully disabled veterans pay nothing for licenses or IDs.

recaps.module: Residency, status and who needs licenses

recap_hooks.text: Residency comes from domicile, voting or filings, while working or studying newcomers face a thirty-day license clock.
Visitors with a home license, students and a few other groups are excused from a Florida license.
Many outside licenses waive both Class E exams, while commercial rules start at the heavy-weight, sixteen-passenger and placarded-cargo lines.

recaps.module: Identity, Social Security and address proof

recap_hooks.text: Bring original identity papers for your status track, proof of your Social Security number and two proofs of address.
Photocopies fail, and a non-citizen may get a short photo-free permit while papers are verified.
Learners start at fifteen and licensed drivers at sixteen, after a clean permit year and logged practice hours.
Disclose impairing conditions and obey every restriction code printed on the license.
An identification card and a driver license are never held together, and offender groups face short registration deadlines.
After a move get a new license within thirty days, and renew with your old card and a vision check.
New licenses and renewals cost forty-eight dollars, replacements twenty-five, and reinstatement fees depend on why the license was lost.
